title: Always pick the best-looking machine?
hook: Always pick the machine that looks best so far. How often does that go wrong?

knows: expected value: 70% of 100 pulls is about 70 wins
that a learner estimates which choice is best from its own results
doesNotKnow: that a learner who only repeats what looks best can lock itself into a worse choice
that a little deliberate random exploration prevents it

misconception: Always choosing the best-looking option is the best strategy.
objective: The learner can explain that a purely greedy learner can be fooled by an unlucky early result and never revisit the better option, while exploring a small fraction of the time costs a little and protects against that.

claims.text: In the toy, machine A pays on 30% of pulls and B on 70%; both players pull A once and B once, then greedy always picks the machine with the better win rate so far (ties to A), and the explorer does the same except on 10% of pulls, when it picks a machine at random.
claims.source: The lesson's own model in Demo.tsx (PAY, play). Payout rates are invented for the toy.

claims.text: Once the explorer has found B it wins about 68 per 100 pulls: 90 pulls on B at 70% (63 wins) plus 10 random pulls at an average 50% (5 wins).
claims.source: 0.9 × 70 + 0.1 × (70 + 30) / 2 = 68. Toy check: over seeds 1-2000 the explorer's pulls 401-500 averaged 67.95 wins and 95.0 pulls on B (node script reproducing play() from Demo.tsx; also computed live in the reveal).

claims.text: In run 1, greedy's single early pull on B lost, so B looked like 0% and greedy never pulled it again, winning about 30 per 100 for all 500 pulls; the stage shows the first pulls (A won, B lost).
claims.source: Run 1 is mulberry32 seed 5, CHOSEN because greedy gets stuck in it (it does not in seeds 1-4). Greedy wins per 100: 40, 29, 23, 30, 41; pulls on B: 1 of 500. The reveal does not generalise from this run; it reports the 2000-run spread (c4). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 16): Own reimplementation and the extracted MODEL block of Demo.tsx agree: seed 5 first pulls are A LOST and B LOST (first = [0,0]); seeds 1-4 and 6 are A lost, B won. The stage prints 'first pulls: A lost, B lost', so the claim's '(A won, B lost)' contradicts the stage. The rest holds: B pulled 1 of 500, wins per 100 = 40, 29, 23, 30, 41 (163/500 = 32.6, 'about 30'), stuck. Since both looked 0%, greedy stayed on A only because ties go to A. Fix (builder): change the parenthetical to '(A lost, B lost; with both at 0% the tie goes to A)'. The reveal text itself is not wrong.

claims.text: In the toy, greedy ends up stuck on A in about 3 runs in 10, winning about 30 per 100 in those runs; the stage tallies how often it was stuck, and the average wins of greedy and the explorer over its last 100 pulls, across the runs the learner watches.
claims.source: Seeds 1-2000 of play() (node script): greedy stuck 30.2% (601 of 604 stuck runs began with B's first pull losing), greedy last-100 mean 57.7, explorer 67.95. The stage's own tallies are computed live from seeds 5 onward. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 16): node, own play() with kit mulberry32, seeds 1-2000: greedy stuck (under 50 B pulls in its last 100) in 30.2%; stuck runs average 29.8 wins in the last 100 and 30.0 per 100 over all 500; 601 of 604 stuck runs began with B's first pull losing; greedy last-100 mean 57.7, explorer 67.95. The learner's default path (Play run 1, Next run, Watch 100 more = seeds 5-106, 102 runs): stuck 33 (32%), greedy 57, explorer 67, so the reveal's hard-coded 'about 3 in 10' sits next to a matching tally.

claims.text: Picking a random option a small fraction of the time and the best-looking one otherwise is the ε-greedy method of reinforcement learning.
claims.source: Sutton & Barto 2018, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed., §2.2-2.3 (ε-greedy action selection; greedy methods can get stuck on suboptimal actions).

recall.question: A music app only ever recommends the genre you have liked most so far. After one bad jazz track early on, it never plays jazz again. What would help it find what you like?
options: Occasionally recommending something it is less sure about
Recommending its current favourite even more often
recall.why: A purely greedy learner trusts early, noisy results and never revisits what looked bad. A little deliberate exploration costs a few plays and lets it discover a better option.
